title: Making Things Hard on Yourself, But in a Good Way: Creating Desirable Difficulties to Enhance Learning https://bjorklab.psych.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/2016/04/EBjork_RBjork_2011.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers the Bjorks' foundational paper coining desirable difficulties — conditions that slow apparent learning but strengthen long-term retention and transfer. The paper's central distinction is between performance (what's observable during instruction) and learning (the durable, permanent change), warning that teaching methods which make performance improve fastest often serve learning worst. It introduces storage strength versus retrieval strength as the mechanism: instruction should aim to build storage strength even when that means retrieval strength develops more slowly. Barton draws out the paper's core instructional recommendations — spacing over massing, interleaving over blocking, retrieval over restudy, and varied over predictable practice conditions — while stressing the Bjorks' key caveat that a difficulty is only desirable if the learner has the background knowledge to actually respond to it successfully.
points: The paper's central warning: conditions that make performance improve quickly often fail to support long-term learning, while conditions that slow apparent progress often optimise it.
Storage strength (how entrenched a memory is) and retrieval strength (its current accessibility) are distinct — good instruction should target the former, not just the latter.
Testing should be treated as a vehicle for learning, not just assessment; repeated testing beats repeated study for durable retention.
A difficulty is only desirable if learners have the necessary background knowledge to respond to it successfully — otherwise it's just an obstacle.
Spacing, interleaving, retrieval practice, and varied practice conditions are the paper's four practical levers for building desirable difficulty into instruction.
quotes: Conditions of learning that make performance improve rapidly often fail to support long-term retention and transfer, whereas conditions that create challenges and slow the rate of apparent learning often optimize long-term retention and transfer
Optimising learning often requires deviating from standard practices and introducing conditions that challenge learners.
Tests should be viewed as a vehicle of learning and not solely a vehicle of assessment.
It is critical to ensure the learner has the necessary background knowledge or skills to respond to the difficulty successfully; otherwise, the challenge becomes an undesirable difficulty.

Instruction should aim to maximise the gain of storage strength (how entrenched a memory is) rather than just rapidly boosting retrieval strength (current accessibility, which dictates immediate performance).
Interleaving, even though it may slow initial performance, leads to superior long-term retention and transfer, potentially by forcing learners to notice similarities and differences among concepts.
